A refrigerator keeps food cold by using a continuous cycle of evaporation and condensation to move heat from the inside of the unit to the outside. A chemical refrigerant flows through coils, absorbing heat from the air inside the fridge and turning into a gas. This gas is then compressed by a compressor, which increases its temperature and pressure, causing it to flow through outdoor coils where it releases that heat into the surrounding room. As the refrigerant cools back into a liquid, it travels back inside to repeat the process, effectively "pumping" heat out of the cabinet to maintain a low internal temperature.

A refrigerator works by moving heat from the inside of the cabinet to the outside environment using a system of coils and a refrigerant. A pump circulates the refrigerant through these coils; as the liquid refrigerant evaporates into a gas inside the fridge, it absorbs heat from the food, cooling the interior. The gas then flows to coils on the outside of the unit, where it is compressed and cooled back into a liquid, releasing the trapped heat into the room. This continuous cycle keeps the internal temperature low by constantly "pumping" heat out of the insulated box.
